opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the clearest places where the difference in approach really shows up. With a video generative model, the output is fundamentally a sequence of 2D frames. Even if you condition on camera motion, you're asking the model to produce pixels that are consistent with some trajectory, and it's doing that implicitly. There's no underlying object in the world that persists. So camera control ends up being sort of a soft constraint. You can say "pan left" or give it a trajectory, and it'll mostly do it, but things drift. If you turn around and come back, the room might not be the same room anymore.

With Marble, what we're generating is an actual 3D representation of the world. Once that world exists, camera control becomes trivial. It's not something the model has to get right, it's just rendering. You can move the camera anywhere you want, as precisely as you want, for as long as you want, and the world stays put. It's consistent by construction rather than consistent because the model learned to approximate consistency.

That changes what you can do with it. If you're a filmmaker or a game developer, you want exact control. You want to frame a shot, do a dolly move at a specific speed, come back to the same angle later and have it match. You want to drop the world into Unity or Blender and integrate it with other tools. That's really hard when your primitive is a video clip and pretty natural when your primitive is a 3D scene.

Now, there are tradeoffs. Video models are very good at dynamics and motion, things changing over time, and that's something an explicit 3D representation doesn't give you for free. So I don't think it's "one is right and one is wrong." But for spatial intelligence, for building worlds you can actually move through and interact with, we think having an explicit, persistent 3D representation is the right foundation, and precise camera control is one of the most immediate benefits you feel.

r001.rationale: It contrasts video models’ soft response to instructions like “pan left” with Marble’s precise, unrestricted camera movement.

r002.rationale: It describes Marble as generating a persistent 3D world that is then rendered, contrasting that with video models’ frame sequences.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually one of the things I think is most fundamental about the difference between the two approaches. With a video model, camera control is something you have to ask for. You're conditioning the generation on some trajectory, and the model is doing its best to produce frames that look like what a camera moving along that path would see. But it's all implicit. The model has some internal, fuzzy notion of 3D structure that it's picked up from training on tons of video, and when you ask it to move the camera, it's essentially hallucinating what the next frame should look like given that motion. Sometimes that works beautifully, and sometimes you pan around and come back and the room is different, or the object you were looking at has quietly changed shape.

With Marble, the output is an actual 3D world. We generate a persistent, explicit 3D representation, Gaussian splats in our case, and once you have that, camera control isn't a generative problem anymore. It's just rendering. You can put the camera anywhere you want, move it however you want, at whatever frame rate you want, and the world stays the same because it actually exists as geometry. There's no drift, no inconsistency, no "the model forgot what was behind you." You walk back and the thing is still there.

So I think of it as the difference between asking a model to imagine a camera move versus having a world and holding a camera in it. The video model is doing something closer to what our brains do when we daydream, which is impressive and flexible but not reliable. Marble is making the world first and then letting you look at it, and that separation is what unlocks things like real-time interaction, editing, physics, all the stuff you want for games or simulation or VR. You can't easily do those things when the 3D structure only lives implicitly in a video model's weights.

That said, I don't think it's an either/or. Video models are incredibly good at dynamics, at motion, at things changing over time. World models like Marble are good at space and persistence. I think a lot of the interesting work over the next few years is going to be about how those two things come together.

r001.rationale: It contrasts trajectory-conditioned video generation with placing and moving a camera freely in Marble, but does not characterize video-model control as qualitative, director-style instructions.

r002.rationale: It describes Marble as generating a persistent 3D world and then rendering views from it, contrasting that with the video model producing frames.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is whether the camera is an explicit control or something you’re asking the model to imagine. With a video generative model, you can prompt it to pan left or move forward, and it can produce a really compelling result. But the camera movement and the content of the scene are being generated together. Asking it to return to exactly the same location or show a particular viewpoint can be difficult.

With Marble, you have a persistent 3D world, and you move a camera through it. You can choose the camera position and orientation, move somewhere, turn around, and come back. The scene stays there. So the camera becomes something you operate directly, rather than something you describe and hope the model interprets the way you intended.

Video models have a lot of flexibility in generating motion and events. But if what you want is to explore a space or precisely compose a shot, having that explicit 3D representation makes a big difference.

r001.rationale: It contrasts prompting video models to move the camera with directly choosing Marble’s camera position and orientation.

r002.rationale: It describes Marble as a persistent 3D world, but does not state that its output is not generated frame by frame.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is whether the camera is moving through a persistent world or whether the model is generating what that movement might look like. With Marble, you have a 3D scene, and you can choose a camera trajectory through it. If you turn around or revisit a location, there’s an underlying scene that determines what you see.

With a video generative model, camera motion is generally part of the generation itself. You can ask for a pan or an orbit, and it can look beautiful, but that’s different from having a camera you can explicitly position in a consistent 3D world.

So there’s a difference between directing a shot and actually operating a camera. Both are useful, but if you want to explore a space or try several shots in the same environment, that explicit control becomes really valuable.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts requesting a pan or orbit as part of video generation with explicitly positioning a camera along a trajectory in Marble’s consistent 3D scene.

r002.rationale: The response describes Marble as having an underlying 3D scene, but does not state that its output is not generated frame by frame.
